title: Common Traits
intro: Almost every type you write needs the same few abilities: print, copy, compare, use as a key, start from a default, convert. Each one is a standard trait. `#[derive(...)]` writes the obvious ones from the fields, and you write the rest by hand.

coming_from.go: Go gives a struct `==` (when every field is comparable), map-key use and `%v` printing without being asked. Rust makes each one a trait you ask for, usually in one `derive` line. `String()` is `impl Display`, and `cmp.Compare` is `Ord::cmp` (floats use `total_cmp`).
coming_from.kotlin: A `data class` writes `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy`. In Rust you list the traits you want: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]`. `Comparable<T>` is `Ord`, and a hand-written `toString()` is `impl Display`.
coming_from.python: `__eq__`, `__hash__`, `__repr__`, `__str__` and `__lt__` become `PartialEq`/`Eq`, `Hash`, `Debug`, `Display` and `PartialOrd`/`Ord`. `@dataclass(order=True, frozen=True)` is the closest thing to one `derive` line. A bare Rust struct has none of them.
coming_from.typescript: A class compares by identity and has no ordering, and a `Map` keys objects by identity too. In Rust a `derive` line gives equality, ordering and hashing by value, and `toString()` is `impl Display`.
coming_from.java: `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `compareTo` become `PartialEq`/`Eq`, `Hash`, `Debug`/`Display` and `Ord`. A `record` writes the first three for you; in Rust the same job is `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Debug)]`, so `equals` and `hashCode` cannot disagree.
coming_from.csharp: `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString` and `IComparable<T>` become `PartialEq`/`Eq`, `Hash`, `Debug`/`Display` and `Ord`. A `record` writes the first three; in Rust you list them in a `derive` line.
coming_from.c: C has no traits. A struct has no `==`, cannot be printed and has no hash, so each one is a function you write and call by name (`qsort` takes a comparison function). A Rust trait is that function, named once and found by the compiler.
coming_from.cpp: `= default` on `operator==` and `operator<=>` is the nearest thing to a derive. A copy constructor is `Clone`, but it runs only at `.clone()`: `b = a` moves. A destructor is `Drop`, and a `std::hash` specialisation is `Hash`. In Rust all of them are traits with fixed names.

notes: `derive` writes the obvious code from the fields. `Display` cannot be derived, because there is no obvious text: you write `impl Display`, and `to_string()` comes with it.
`Debug` (`{:?}`) is for developers and `Display` (`{}`) is for users. A type has neither until you add it.
Some traits need others. `Eq` needs `PartialEq`, `Ord` needs `PartialOrd` and `Eq`, and `Copy` needs `Clone`.
`f64` has `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd` but not `Eq`, `Ord` or `Hash`, because `NaN` is not equal to itself. A struct with an `f64` field cannot derive them either.

gotcha.title: Using your own type as a map key
gotcha.looks_fine: Most languages let a small data type be a map key right away, or after a one-word change. You put `Version(1, 2)` in, ask for `Version(1, 2)` back, and expect it to be found.
gotcha.rust_sees: A `HashMap` key needs `Eq` and `Hash`, and `Version` has neither. Nothing is derived unless you ask. The compiler lists the missing traits and suggests the `derive`.
gotcha.why: A key is compared and hashed, and for your own type Rust will not guess what "the same" means. Asking for `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` says that two versions are the same when every field is. It is one line, and it keeps `==` and the hash in step.

go.says: Go prints `found: stable true`. A struct whose fields are all comparable can be a map key with nothing declared. A struct with a slice field cannot, and that is a compile error (the page shows it).

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints `found: stable`, because a `data class` writes `equals` and `hashCode`. A plain `class` would not, and the lookup would find nothing (the page runs one).

python.says: Python prints `found: stable`. A frozen dataclass writes `__eq__` and `__hash__`. A plain class compares by identity, so the lookup finds nothing (the page runs one).

typescript.says: TypeScript compiles this and prints `found: undefined`. A `Map` compares object keys by identity, so the second `new Version(1, 2)` is a different key. Key on a string built from the fields, or keep the one object.

java.says: Java prints `found: stable`, because a `record` writes `equals` and `hashCode`. A plain class without them finds nothing (the page runs one).

csharp.says: C# prints `found: stable`, because a `record` writes `Equals` and `GetHashCode`. A plain class without them finds nothing (the page runs one).

c.says: C has no standard hash map type, so there is nothing to try. A table you write or borrow decides for itself how keys are hashed and compared.

cpp.says: C++ refuses too. `std::unordered_map` needs a `std::hash<Version>`. The error says the `unordered_map` constructor is a deleted function, and it is long because it is reported from inside the library; look for `std::hash<Version>` in it. A `std::map` needs only an `operator<`.

python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass


# order=True writes <, > from the fields in order; frozen=True makes it hashable.
@dataclass(order=True, frozen=True)
class Version:
    major: int = 0
    minor: int = 0

    # __str__ is the user-facing text (the dataclass's __repr__ is the debug text).
    def __str__(self):
        return f"v{self.major}.{self.minor}"


a = Version(1, 10)
b = Version(1, 9)
print("display:", a)
print("a == b:", str(a == b).lower())
print("a > b:", str(a > b).lower())

all_versions = sorted([a, b, Version()])
print("sorted:", " ".join(str(v) for v in all_versions))

seen = set()
for v in [a, b, Version(), a]:
    seen.add(v)
print("distinct:", len(seen))
